subject: history
topicDisplay: Challenges for Britain, Europe and the wider world 1901 to the present day
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 history question on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: The First World War 1914-18 and its causes
The Peace Settlement and the Treaty of Versailles
The end of the British Empire and decolonisation
Britain's place in the world since 1945
Chronology, causation and using historical evidence

questions.lo: The First World War 1914-18 and its causes
questions.q: In which years was the First World War fought?
questions.explain: The First World War lasted from 1914 to 1918. It ended with an armistice on 11 November 1918.

questions.lo: The First World War 1914-18 and its causes
questions.q: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914 is best described as which kind of cause of the First World War?
options: A long-term cause building up for decades
questions.explain: The assassination was the short-term trigger, or 'spark'. The long-term causes were militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism, which had built up tension over many years.

questions.lo: The First World War 1914-18 and its causes
questions.q: Which of these is one of the main long-term causes of the First World War?
options: The system of alliances between countries
The fall of the Berlin Wall
questions.explain: Alliances split Europe into two armed camps, so a conflict between two countries could quickly drag in many others. Militarism, imperialism and nationalism were the other long-term causes.

questions.lo: The Peace Settlement and the Treaty of Versailles
questions.q: What was the Treaty of Versailles (1919)?
options: An alliance between Britain and Germany
The peace settlement that punished Germany after the First World War
A trade deal with the USA
The treaty that started the Cold War
questions.explain: The Treaty of Versailles was the 1919 peace settlement. It blamed Germany for the war and forced it to pay reparations, lose land and reduce its armed forces.

questions.lo: The Peace Settlement and the Treaty of Versailles
questions.q: Why do many historians link the Treaty of Versailles to the outbreak of the Second World War?
options: It made Germany rich and powerful
Its harsh terms caused resentment that Hitler later exploited
It had no effect on Germany
questions.explain: The treaty's harsh terms left many Germans feeling humiliated and angry. Hitler used this resentment to build support, so historians see a causal chain from Versailles to the rise of the Nazis and the Second World War.

questions.q: In which year did women in Britain finally win the vote on equal terms with men, at age 21?
questions.explain: Some women (over 30 and meeting a property rule) got the vote in 1918. Full equality with men, at age 21, came in 1928.

questions.q: What was the main difference between the suffragists and the suffragettes?
options: The suffragists were peaceful while the suffragettes used more militant direct action
The suffragettes did not want the vote
questions.explain: Both wanted votes for women. The suffragists (led by Millicent Fawcett) used peaceful methods; the suffragettes (led by Emmeline Pankhurst) used more militant direct action.

questions.q: Why did dictators gain support in some countries during the 1930s?
options: Economic hardship in the Great Depression made people accept leaders who promised jobs, order and pride
They promised more freedom and democracy
questions.explain: The Great Depression brought mass unemployment and hardship. Dictators such as Hitler and Mussolini promised jobs, order and national pride, so many desperate people supported them despite the loss of freedom.

questions.q: In which year did the Second World War begin, when Britain and France declared war after Germany invaded Poland?
questions.explain: The Second World War began in September 1939 when Germany invaded Poland. It ended in 1945.

questions.q: What was 'the Blitz'?
options: The German bombing of British cities in 1940-41
questions.explain: The Blitz was the sustained German bombing of British cities. The experience of ordinary people during the war is often called the 'Home Front'.

questions.q: Who was Britain's Prime Minister for most of the Second World War?
questions.explain: Winston Churchill led Britain as Prime Minister for most of the Second World War and is remembered for his wartime speeches.

questions.q: Which statement most accurately describes the Holocaust?
options: The systematic, state-organised murder of around six million Jewish people, alongside other targeted groups
A natural disaster during the war
questions.explain: The Holocaust was a deliberate, systematic genocide carried out by the Nazi state: the planned murder of around six million Jewish people, along with Roma and Sinti people, disabled people and others. It must be described accurately and respectfully.

questions.q: The Holocaust did not happen all at once. Which sequence best shows how it developed?
options: Prejudice and propaganda, then laws removing rights, then ghettos, then mass murder in camps
A single day of violence, then nothing
questions.explain: The Holocaust grew in stages: from prejudice and propaganda, to laws stripping Jewish people of their rights, to ghettos, and finally to mass murder in death camps such as Auschwitz. Understanding this shows how unchallenged hatred can escalate.

questions.q: Which two superpowers were the main rivals during the Cold War?
options: The USA and the USSR (Soviet Union)
questions.explain: The Cold War (roughly 1947-1991) was a rivalry between the capitalist USA and the communist USSR (Soviet Union).

questions.q: Why is the Cold War described as 'cold'?
options: It was fought in very cold weather
The USA and USSR never fought each other directly; it was tension, an arms race and rivalry
Only one small battle took place
It happened at the North Pole
questions.explain: It is 'cold' because the two superpowers never fought each other face-to-face. It was a stand-off of tension, spying and an arms race, kept from turning 'hot' partly by the fear of nuclear war.

questions.lo: The end of the British Empire and decolonisation
questions.q: What word do historians use for the process of colonies becoming independent from an empire?
questions.explain: Decolonisation is the process of colonies gaining independence. For Britain this sped up after 1945, beginning with India in 1947.

questions.lo: The end of the British Empire and decolonisation
questions.q: Which country's independence in 1947 was a major turning point in the end of the British Empire?
questions.explain: India became independent in 1947, a huge turning point. Over the following decades many African and Caribbean nations also gained independence.

questions.q: Why did Britain encourage people from the Commonwealth to come to Britain after 1945?
options: To fight in the First World War
Britain needed workers to rebuild and to staff new services like the NHS
questions.explain: After the war Britain had to rebuild and lacked workers, including for the new NHS (founded 1948). It invited people from the Commonwealth, such as the Windrush generation from the Caribbean, helping create modern multicultural Britain.

questions.lo: Britain's place in the world since 1945
questions.q: Which international organisation, focused on trade and cooperation in Europe, did the UK join in 1973 (later becoming the European Union)?
questions.explain: The UK joined the European Economic Community (EEC) in 1973. It later became the European Union (EU), which the UK voted to leave in 2016 and formally left in 2020.

questions.lo: Chronology, causation and using historical evidence
questions.q: A historian studies a wartime government propaganda poster and calls it 'biased'. What should they do with it?
options: Ignore it, because biased sources are useless
Still use it, as useful evidence of what the government wanted people to think and do
Only trust it if it is a photograph
Never trust any source from the time
questions.explain: Even a biased source is useful evidence. A propaganda poster tells us what the government wanted people to believe. Historians question sources for reliability and purpose rather than simply discarding them.
